paragraphs: On an unusually hot evening in early July, a young man came out of the tiny attic room he rented in S. Place and walked slowly, as if hesitating, toward K. Bridge.

He had managed to avoid running into his landlady on the stairs. His attic was under the roof of a tall, five-story building and was more like a cupboard than a room. The landlady, who provided his room, his dinners, and his laundry, lived on the floor below, and every time he went out he had to pass her kitchen, whose door always stood open. And each time he passed, the young man felt a sick, frightened feeling that made him scowl and feel ashamed. He was hopelessly in debt to his landlady and was afraid of meeting her.

This wasn’t because he was cowardly or spineless, quite the opposite. But for some time he had been in an overstrained, irritable state bordering on hypochondria. He had become so completely wrapped up in himself and cut off from other people that he dreaded meeting not only his landlady but anyone at all. Poverty had crushed him, but the worries of his situation had lately stopped weighing on him. He had given up dealing with practical matters. He had lost all desire to. No landlady could do anything that truly frightened him. But to be stopped on the stairs, to be forced to listen to her petty, irrelevant gossip, her nagging demands for payment, her threats and complaints, and to rack his brains for excuses, to dodge, to lie? No. Rather than that, he would creep down the stairs like a cat and slip out unseen.
This evening, however, as he came out into the street, he became sharply aware of his fears.

“I want to attempt a thing like that, and I’m frightened by these trifles,” he thought with an odd smile. “Hm, yes. Everything is in a man’s hands, and he lets it all slip out of cowardice. That’s an axiom. It would be interesting to know what men are most afraid of. Taking a new step, saying a new word, that’s what they fear most. But I’m talking too much. It’s because I chatter that I do nothing. Or maybe I chatter because I do nothing. I’ve learned to chatter this past month, lying for days on end in my den, thinking of Jack the Giant-Killer. Why am I going there now? Am I capable of that? Is it even serious? It isn’t serious at all. It’s just a fantasy to amuse myself, a toy! Yes, maybe it is a toy.”

The heat in the street was terrible, and the airlessness, the bustle, and the plaster, scaffolding, bricks, and dust all around him, and that special Petersburg stench so familiar to everyone who can’t leave town in summer, all worked painfully on the young man’s already overwrought nerves. The unbearable smell from the taverns, which are especially numerous in that part of the city, and the drunken men he kept meeting, even though it was a workday, completed the revolting misery of the picture. For a moment an expression of the deepest disgust flashed across the young man’s refined face. He was, by the way, exceptionally handsome, taller than average, slim and well built, with beautiful dark eyes and dark brown hair. Soon he sank into deep thought, or more precisely into a complete blankness of mind. He walked along without noticing what was around him and not wanting to. From time to time he muttered something, from the habit of talking to himself, which he had just admitted. At these moments he became aware that his thoughts were sometimes in a tangle and that he was very weak. For two days he had barely tasted food.

He was so badly dressed that even a man used to shabbiness would have been ashamed to be seen in the street in such rags. In that part of town, however, hardly any flaw in dress would have caused surprise. Because of the nearness of the Haymarket, the number of disreputable establishments, and the crowds of tradesmen and laborers packed into these streets and alleys in the heart of Petersburg, such various types were seen that no figure, however odd, would have drawn attention. But there was so much accumulated bitterness and contempt in the young man’s heart that, despite all the fussiness of youth, he minded his rags least of all in the street. It was a different matter when he met acquaintances or former fellow students, whom, indeed, he disliked meeting at any time. And yet when a drunken man, who for some unknown reason was being driven somewhere in a huge cart pulled by a heavy dray horse, suddenly shouted at him as he drove by, “Hey there, German hatter!” bawling at the top of his voice and pointing at him, the young man stopped suddenly and clutched his hat with a trembling hand. It was a tall round hat from Zimmerman’s, but completely worn out, rusty with age, torn and spattered, brimless and bent to one side in a most unseemly way. Not shame, however, but quite another feeling, akin to terror, had overtaken him.

“I knew it,” he muttered in confusion. “I thought so! That’s the worst of all! Why, a stupid thing like this, the most trivial detail, could spoil the whole plan. Yes, my hat is too noticeable. It looks absurd, and that makes it noticeable. With my rags I should wear a cap, any sort of old pancake, but not this grotesque thing. Nobody wears a hat like this. It would be noticed a mile off, it would be remembered. What matters is that people would remember it, and that would give them a clue. For this business one should be as inconspicuous as possible. Trifles, trifles are what matter! Why, it’s exactly such trifles that always ruin everything.”

He didn’t have far to go. He knew, in fact, exactly how many steps it was from the gate of his lodging house: seven hundred and thirty. He had counted them once when he was lost in dreams. At the time he had put no faith in those dreams and was only teasing himself with their hideous but daring recklessness. Now, a month later, he had begun to look at them differently, and despite the monologues in which he jeered at his own weakness and indecision, he had involuntarily come to regard this “hideous” dream as a feat to be attempted, though he still didn’t admit this to himself. He was actually going now for a “rehearsal” of his project, and with every step his excitement grew more and more violent.

With a sinking heart and a nervous tremor, he went up to a huge house that faced the canal on one side and the street on the other. This house was divided into tiny apartments and was inhabited by working people of all kinds: tailors, locksmiths, cooks, assorted Germans, girls picking up a living as best they could, petty clerks, and so on. There was a constant coming and going through the two gates and in the two courtyards of the house. Three or four doormen were employed in the building. The young man was very glad to meet none of them and slipped unnoticed through the door on the right and up the staircase. It was a back staircase, dark and narrow, but he already knew it well and knew his way, and he liked all these surroundings. In such darkness even the most inquisitive eyes weren’t to be feared.

“If I’m so scared now, what would it be like if I somehow actually went through with it?” he couldn’t help asking himself as he reached the fourth floor. There his way was blocked by some porters who were carrying furniture out of an apartment. He knew the apartment had been occupied by a German civil service clerk and his family. The German was moving out, and so the fourth floor of this staircase would be empty except for the old woman. “That’s a good thing anyway,” he thought, as he rang the bell of the old woman’s apartment. The bell gave a faint tinkle, as though it were made of tin and not brass. The little apartments in such houses always have bells that ring like that. He had forgotten the sound of that bell, and now its peculiar tinkle seemed to remind him of something and bring it clearly before him. He started. His nerves were terribly overstrained by now. In a little while the door was opened a tiny crack. The old woman eyed her visitor with obvious distrust through the crack, and nothing could be seen but her little eyes glittering in the darkness. But seeing several people on the landing, she grew bolder and opened the door wide. The young man stepped into the dark entry, which was partitioned off from the tiny kitchen. The old woman stood facing him in silence, looking at him questioningly. She was a tiny, withered old woman of sixty, with sharp, spiteful eyes and a sharp little nose. Her colorless, somewhat graying hair was thickly smeared with oil, and she wore no kerchief over it. Around her long, thin neck, which looked like a hen’s leg, was knotted some sort of flannel rag, and despite the heat, a mangy fur cape, yellow with age, hung flapping on her shoulders. The old woman coughed and groaned constantly. The young man must have looked at her with a rather peculiar expression, because a gleam of mistrust came into her eyes again.
“Raskolnikov, a student. I came here a month ago,” the young man hurried to mutter, with a half bow, remembering that he ought to be more polite.
“I remember, my good sir, I remember quite well your coming here,” the old woman said distinctly, still keeping her questioning eyes on his face.

“And here, I’m again on the same errand,” Raskolnikov continued, a little disconcerted and surprised at the old woman’s mistrust. “Maybe she’s always like that, though, and I just didn’t notice it the other time,” he thought uneasily.
The old woman paused as if hesitating, then stepped to one side, and pointing to the door of the room, said, letting her visitor go ahead of her:
“Step in, my good sir.”
The little room the young man walked into, with yellow wallpaper, geraniums and muslin curtains in the windows, was brightly lit at that moment by the setting sun.

“So the sun will be shining like this then too!” flashed, as if by chance, through Raskolnikov’s mind, and with a quick glance he took in everything in the room, trying as far as possible to notice and remember its layout. But there was nothing special about the room. The furniture, all very old and made of yellow wood, consisted of a sofa with a huge curved wooden back, an oval table in front of the sofa, a dressing table with a mirror fixed to it between the windows, chairs along the walls, and two or three cheap prints in yellow frames showing German maidens holding birds. That was all. In the corner a light was burning before a small icon. Everything was very clean. The floor and furniture were brightly polished, and everything shone.
“Lizaveta’s work,” thought the young man. There wasn’t a speck of dust to be seen in the whole apartment.

“It’s in the homes of spiteful old widows that you find such cleanliness,” Raskolnikov thought again, and he stole a curious glance at the cotton curtain over the door leading into another tiny room, where the old woman’s bed and chest of drawers stood, and which he had never looked into before. These two rooms made up the whole apartment.
“What do you want?” the old woman said sternly, coming into the room and, as before, standing in front of him so she could look him straight in the face.
“I’ve brought something to pawn,” and he drew out of his pocket an old-fashioned flat silver watch, with a globe engraved on the back. The chain was steel.
“But the time is up on your last pledge. The month was up the day before yesterday.”
“I’ll bring you the interest for another month. Wait a little.”
“But it’s for me to decide, my good sir, whether to wait or sell your pledge right away.”
“How much will you give me for the watch, Alyona Ivanovna?”
“You come with such trifles, my good sir. It’s hardly worth anything. Last time I gave you two rubles for your ring, and you could buy it brand new at a jeweler’s for a ruble and a half.”
“Give me four rubles for it. I’ll redeem it. It was my father’s. I’ll be getting some money soon.”
“A ruble and a half, and the interest in advance, if you like!”
“A ruble and a half!” cried the young man.

“Suit yourself,” and the old woman handed him back the watch. The young man took it and was so angry that he was about to leave, but he stopped himself at once, remembering that there was nowhere else he could go and that he had another purpose in coming.
“Hand it over,” he said roughly.

The old woman fumbled in her pocket for her keys and disappeared behind the curtain into the other room. The young man, left standing alone in the middle of the room, listened curiously, thinking. He could hear her unlocking the chest of drawers.

“It must be the top drawer,” he reflected. “So she carries the keys in her right pocket. All in one bunch on a steel ring. And there’s one key there, three times as big as all the others, with deep notches. That can’t be the key to the chest of drawers. So there must be some other chest or strongbox. That’s worth knowing. Strongboxes always have keys like that. But how degrading it all is.”
The old woman came back.

“Here, sir. Since we say ten kopecks per ruble per month, I have to take fifteen kopecks from a ruble and a half for the month in advance. But for the two rubles I lent you before, you now owe me twenty kopecks in advance on the same reckoning. That makes thirty-five kopecks altogether. So I must give you a ruble and fifteen kopecks for the watch. Here it is.”
“What! Only a ruble and fifteen kopecks now!”
“Just so.”
The young man didn’t argue and took the money. He looked at the old woman and was in no hurry to leave, as though there were something more he wanted to say or do, though he didn’t quite know what.
“I may be bringing you something else in a day or two, Alyona Ivanovna, something valuable, silver, a cigarette case, as soon as I get it back from a friend,” he broke off in confusion.
“Well, we’ll talk about it then, sir.”
“Goodbye. Are you always at home alone? Your sister isn’t here with you?” he asked as casually as possible as he went out into the passage.
“What business is she of yours, my good sir?”
“Oh, nothing in particular, I just asked. You’re too quick. Good day, Alyona Ivanovna.”

Raskolnikov went out in complete confusion. This confusion grew more and more intense. As he went down the stairs, he even stopped short two or three times, as though suddenly struck by some thought. When he was in the street, he cried out, “Oh, God, how loathsome it all is! Can I, can I possibly. No, it’s nonsense, it’s rubbish!” he added resolutely. “And how could such an atrocious thing come into my head? What filthy things my heart is capable of. Yes, filthy above all, disgusting, loathsome, loathsome! And for a whole month I’ve been.” But no words, no exclamations could express his agitation. The feeling of intense repulsion, which had begun to oppress and torture his heart on the way to the old woman’s, had by now reached such a pitch and taken such a definite shape that he didn’t know what to do with himself to escape his misery. He walked along the pavement like a drunk, ignoring the passersby and bumping into them, and came to his senses only in the next street. Looking around, he noticed he was standing near a tavern entered by steps leading from the pavement down to the basement. At that instant two drunken men came out the door and, abusing and holding each other up, climbed the steps. Without stopping to think, Raskolnikov went down the steps at once. Until that moment he had never been inside a tavern, but now he felt dizzy and was tormented by a burning thirst. He longed for a drink of cold beer and put his sudden weakness down to lack of food. He sat down at a sticky little table in a dark, dirty corner, ordered some beer, and eagerly drank off the first glass. At once he felt easier, and his thoughts became clear.

“All that’s nonsense,” he said hopefully, “and there’s nothing in it to worry about! It’s simply physical disorder. Just a glass of beer, a piece of dry bread, and in a moment the brain is stronger, the mind is clearer, and the will is firm! Phew, how utterly petty it all is!”

But despite this scornful reflection, he now looked cheerful, as though he had suddenly been freed from a terrible burden, and he gazed around in a friendly way at the people in the room. But even at that moment he had a dim foreboding that this happier frame of mind wasn’t normal either.

There were few people in the tavern at the time. Besides the two drunken men he had met on the steps, a group of about five men and a girl with a concertina had gone out at the same time. Their departure left the room quiet and rather empty. The people still in the tavern were a man who seemed to be a craftsman, drunk but not extremely so, sitting in front of a pot of beer, and his companion, a huge, stout man with a gray beard, in a short, full-skirted coat. He was very drunk and had fallen asleep on the bench. Every now and then, as if in his sleep, he started cracking his fingers, with his arms spread wide and the upper part of his body bouncing around on the bench, while he hummed some meaningless refrain, trying to recall lines like these:
“His wife a year he fondly loved, His wife a—a year he—fondly loved.”
Or suddenly waking up again:
“Walking along the crowded row, He met the one he used to know.”

But no one shared his enjoyment. His silent companion watched all these displays with positive hostility and mistrust. There was another man in the room who looked something like a retired government clerk. He sat apart, now and then sipping from his mug and looking around at the company. He, too, seemed to be somewhat agitated.
